---
title: "Proposal Overview"
---

## Summary

**Problem.** Drug shortages disrupt patient care and impose large costs on hospitals and
pharmacies. Warning time before a shortage is declared is highly variable, which makes
preparation expensive and poorly targeted.

**Goal.** Determine whether shortage onset can be anticipated from public federal data, and
identify which supply-side signals carry advance warning. The project produces a calibrated
probability that a given drug enters shortage within a defined window, together with evidence
about which product characteristics drive that risk.

**Unit of analysis.** Active ingredient &times; route of administration — 2,897 approved prescription
units.

**Validation.** Temporal only: train on earlier years, test on later ones.

## Planned Data Sources

| Dataset | Provider | Role | Approx. size |
|---|---|---|---|
| Archived CDER shortage CSVs | Internet Archive | Labels: onset and resolution dates | 102 captures, 2019–2026 |
| Drug Shortages (live) | openFDA | Current shortage state, NDC keys | 1,634 records |
| NSDE product lifecycle | openFDA | Supply-side panel; retains delisted products | 667,457 records |
| NDC Directory | openFDA | Product master, route and dosage form | 137,733 records |
| Drug Enforcement (recalls) | openFDA | Recall history | 17,899 records |
| Orange Book | FDA | Approval type, ANDA counts | 48,663 products |
| Medicare Part B / Part D | CMS | Demand, price trend, manufacturer counts | 15,335 rows |

All sources are US federal public-domain data, available as bulk downloads without
authentication. Total download is approximately 100 MB. The NDC product code is the primary join
key.

## Current Research Questions

The five questions are stated in full on the [Research Questions](questions.qmd) page. In brief: whether
manufacturers exit before shortages are declared (RQ1); which characteristics distinguish
shortage-prone drugs (RQ2); how predictable onset is under temporal validation (RQ3); and whether
that predictability survives changes in the dominant causes of shortage (RQ4).

## Major Constraints

**The live shortage file is a snapshot, not a history.** FDA purges resolved shortages after
approximately six months. Labels must be reconstructed from archived captures; this is done, but
it introduces its own coverage limits (below).

**Short shortages are under-represented.** The archived capture series has two gaps exceeding
FDA's purge window, and the median lag between a record's posting date and the first capture
containing it is 116 days. Episodes that open and close between captures are invisible. Both
effects bias the recovered record toward longer shortages, and we report this rather than
treating the panel as complete.

**Target leakage is a documented, severe risk on this task.** Any feature derived from how long a
record has been posted predicts the label almost perfectly while being useless in practice. The
team fixes a banned-feature list before modeling and treats unexpectedly high performance as a
leakage bug until proven otherwise.

**The process is not stationary.** FDA's attribution of shortage causes inverts between reporting
periods, so results are reported by period rather than pooled.

**Licensing.** openFDA and CDER data are public domain and freely redistributable. ASHP /
University of Utah shortage bulletins are copyrighted for personal use only; they are not used or
redistributed in this project.

## Changes Since Milestone 0

The approved Milestone 0 proposal remains the basis of this project.

**Related work was identified and the contribution sharpened.** Two public GitHub projects
attempt a similar reconstruction. Neither is peer-reviewed and neither covers the full approved
prescription universe. The [Background](background.qmd) page states what they establish and where
this project differs — principally the full ingredient &times; route universe rather than a WHO
Essential Medicines List subset, and the use of NSDE supply-side lifecycle data that neither
project employs. This improves focus by making the contribution explicit rather than assumed.
